prompt: `thumbs` raises an exception on an event from S3. Who tries the event again?

choices.text: Lambda, from its own queue, twice by default
choices.why: S3 invokes asynchronously: Lambda accepted the event and owns the retries, as the function's settings say.

choices.text: S3, which sends the notification again
choices.why: S3 was answered at once that the event was accepted; it does not wait to see the function's result.

choices.text: Nobody: an asynchronous event is tried once
choices.why: That describes no source. Asynchronous events get Lambda's retries; it is a synchronous caller that gets none from Lambda.

choices.text: The event source mapping, through the visibility timeout
choices.why: Mappings belong to pollers such as SQS. A bucket notification is a push, with no mapping in between.

prompt: Match each source with what happens when the function fails on its event.

pairs.right: the caller is told, and decides whether to try again
Lambda retries from its own queue, then a destination
the mapping retries and holds the shard

right_distractors: the record is deleted on the first failure
S3 resends until the object is deleted

prompt: An asynchronous function has no destination and no dead-letter queue. An event fails all three attempts. What is left of it?

choices.text: It waits in Lambda's queue until somebody replays it
choices.why: Lambda drops the event once the retries or the maximum age are used up; there is no replay of a dropped event.

choices.text: Lines in the function's log, and nothing else
choices.why: Without a destination, the error lines are the only trace; that is why the destination is the first setting to look for.

choices.text: The source is notified and sends it again later
choices.why: An asynchronous source was told the event was accepted, and hears nothing about how it went.

choices.text: A copy in the function's default SQS queue
choices.why: There is no default queue; a destination exists only if somebody configured one.

prompt: With Lambda's default asynchronous settings, a function that fails on every attempt receives one S3 event. How many times does the function run for it?
hint: The first attempt, then the retries.

prompt: `thumbs` charges the customer one credit per thumbnail and then fails on a timeout writing its log. Lambda retries the event. What protects the customer from paying twice?

choices.text: Setting the maximum retry attempts to zero
choices.why: That turns every transient failure into a lost thumbnail, and an event may still arrive twice from the source.

choices.text: An on-failure destination
choices.why: A destination receives events that failed every attempt; it does nothing about an attempt that half succeeded.

choices.text: An idempotent handler
choices.why: Retries mean the same event can run twice; a handler that records each charge by bucket, key and eTag, and skips one it already made, is safe to run twice.

choices.text: Invoking it synchronously from S3 instead
choices.why: S3 has no synchronous mode for notifications; the shape comes with the source.

prompt: On AWS, you save a bucket notification to `thumbs` before running `add-permission`. What happens?

choices.text: It is saved, and uploads invoke the function anyway
choices.why: S3 needs the function's policy to let it in, and checks for it when the configuration is saved.

choices.text: It is saved, and the function adds the permission itself
choices.why: Nothing adds a permission on its own; it is an explicit statement somebody writes.

choices.text: It is saved, and only the first upload fails
choices.why: The check happens when the configuration is saved, before any upload.

choices.text: It is refused: S3 cannot validate the destination
choices.why: S3 checks that the function's policy lets it invoke, and fails with `Unable to validate the following destination configurations`. moto skipped that check.

prompt: Why does the permission for S3 carry `AWS:SourceAccount` as well as the bucket's ARN?

choices.text: Bucket names are global
choices.why: If the bucket were deleted and its name taken by another account, the ARN would match that bucket; the account condition stops it.

choices.text: Lambda refuses a permission with only one condition
choices.why: One condition is valid; the second is there for what it prevents.

choices.text: It lets every bucket in the account invoke the function
choices.why: It narrows rather than widens: both conditions must hold.

choices.text: S3 sends the account instead of the ARN in its event
choices.why: The event carries the bucket's name and ARN; the condition concerns who invokes, not what the event says.

prompt: After the section pointed the bucket at the SQS queue, an upload to `uploads/` reached the queue and not `thumbs`. Why?

choices.text: S3 sends each event to one destination type only
choices.why: A bucket can notify several destinations at once, in one configuration that lists them all.

choices.text: The second call replaced the whole configuration
choices.why: `put-bucket-notification-configuration` writes the entire set; the Lambda entry was not in the new one, so it was gone.

choices.text: moto runs no function, so it dropped the Lambda entry
choices.why: moto ran no function either way, but the Lambda entry vanished because the new call left it out, as on AWS.

choices.text: A queue takes priority over a function for the same prefix
choices.why: There is no priority between destination types. Two destinations with overlapping filters for the same event type are refused.

prompt: In S3's event the object key `uploads%2Fcat.jpg` is URL-___, so the handler passes it through `unquote_plus` before asking S3 for the object.
`thumbs` is triggered by `ObjectCreated` under `uploads/` and writes each thumbnail to `uploads/thumbs/`. What happens after the first photo?

choices.text: Nothing unusual: S3 does not notify for objects a function wrote
choices.why: S3 notifies for every object created under the prefix, whoever wrote it.

choices.text: The thumbnail fails, because `/var/task` is read-only
choices.why: The function writes to S3 through the API, not to its own disk.

choices.text: A thumbnail of the thumbnail, and so on: the function calls itself
choices.why: Each thumbnail is an `ObjectCreated` event under `uploads/`, which triggers the function again. Another prefix or bucket breaks the loop.

choices.text: S3 refuses to save the configuration once it detects the loop
choices.why: S3 does not analyse what a function writes; the configuration is accepted.

prompt: Put in order what happens to the three messages of the section's batch on AWS, with ReportBatchItemFailures on the mapping.
items: The mapping receives the three messages from the queue
Lambda invokes orders with the batch as one event
The handler answers with batchItemFailures naming m-2
Lambda deletes m-1 and m-3 from the queue
m-2 becomes visible again when its visibility timeout ends
trap: Deleting the messages before the function answers: the mapping only knows which ones to delete once it has read the response.

prompt: `orders.py` returns `{"batchItemFailures": [{"itemIdentifier": "m-2"}]}`, but the mapping was created without `--function-response-types ReportBatchItemFailures`. What happens to `m-2`?

choices.text: It comes back, like any failed message
choices.why: Only an exception fails a batch here. A normal return is success, whatever it contains.

choices.text: The whole batch comes back, since an answer was not understood
choices.why: The mapping does not read the answer at all without the setting, so there is nothing for it to misunderstand.

choices.text: It goes straight to the dead-letter queue
choices.why: Nothing failed as far as the mapping knows, so nothing is redriven.

choices.text: It is deleted with the others, unread
choices.why: The answer is ignored, the batch counts as a success, and all three messages are deleted.

prompt: A queue receives 600 messages a minute, steadily, and the mapping has a batch size of 10 and full batches every time. How many invocations a minute does that make?
A stream mapping has no retry limit, no bisecting and no destination. One record makes the handler raise every time. What happens to that shard?

choices.text: Its shard stops until the record expires
choices.why: The mapping retries the batch to keep the shard's order, and only the record's expiry, a day on DynamoDB Streams, ends it.

choices.text: The record is skipped after two retries, as with S3
choices.why: Two retries are the asynchronous default; a stream mapping retries until told otherwise.

choices.text: The record moves to a dead-letter queue
choices.why: A stream has no visibility timeout or redrive policy; a destination only exists if configured.

choices.text: The other records of the batch are processed and the bad one is retried alone
choices.why: That is what bisecting would do, and this mapping has none.

prompt: Which settings limit what one bad record does to a stream shard? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `--maximum-retry-attempts`
choices.why: It makes the mapping give up on a batch after so many retries.

choices.text: `--bisect-batch-on-function-error`
choices.why: It splits a failing batch so the bad record ends up alone and the rest get through.

choices.text: An on-failure destination
choices.why: It keeps a description of the records given up on, so they are examined instead of lost.

choices.text: A longer visibility timeout
choices.why: Visibility timeouts belong to SQS queues; a stream has none.

choices.text: A larger `--batch-size`
choices.why: A larger batch puts more good records behind the bad one, and limits nothing.

prompt: Under `pattern.json`, an event arrives with `source` `shop.payments`, `detail-type` `OrderPlaced` and a total of 1500. Does the rule match?

choices.text: Yes: the total is over 1000
choices.why: The total passes, but every field the pattern names must match, and `source` does not.

choices.text: No: `source` is not `shop.orders`
choices.why: Every field the pattern lists must match; `A-3` failed on exactly this.

choices.text: Yes: two of the three fields match
choices.why: A pattern is not a vote; one field that fails is enough to miss.

choices.text: No: `detail-type` should be in `detail`
choices.why: `detail-type` is a top-level field of every event, where the pattern looks for it.

prompt: `aws events test-event-pattern` printed nothing and exited with status 0. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The event matches, since there was no error
choices.why: On AWS a match is `{"Result": true}`; silence is not an answer either way.

choices.text: The pattern is invalid
choices.why: An invalid pattern is an error with a message, and the exit status says so.

choices.text: That moto leaves the call unanswered
choices.why: moto 5.2.3 lists the call and implements nothing behind it; on AWS this event gives `{"Result": false}`.

choices.text: The event does not match, since nothing was delivered
choices.why: `test-event-pattern` delivers nothing in any case; it only answers a question.

prompt: A colleague writes the pattern with `"detail_type": ["OrderPlaced"]`, underscore instead of hyphen. What does EventBridge do?

choices.text: Corrects it to `detail-type`
choices.why: EventBridge matches field names exactly and guesses nothing.

choices.text: Refuses the rule as invalid
choices.why: Any field name is legal in a pattern; one that no event carries is not an error.

choices.text: Ignores the unknown field and matches on the rest
choices.why: A field the pattern names must be present and match; it is not skipped.

choices.text: Accepts it, and the rule never matches anything
choices.why: No event has a `detail_type` field, so every event fails the pattern, silently. Testing against real events finds it.

prompt: The shop adds a loyalty function that must see every `OrderPlaced`, of any total. What changes in the checkout's code?

choices.text: Nothing; a second rule does it
choices.why: The publisher names nobody, so a new consumer is a new rule and target, with no change to who publishes.

choices.text: It publishes each event twice, once per function
choices.why: That is the coupling EventBridge removes; one event can match several rules.

choices.text: It calls the new function directly after publishing
choices.why: Then the checkout knows its consumers again, and waits for one of them.

choices.text: It adds the function's ARN to each event's `resources`
choices.why: `resources` describes what the event is about; it does not route it.

prompt: Under `pattern.json`, five events are published, all from `shop.orders`: `OrderPlaced` with totals 1000, 1000.01 and 2500, `OrderCancelled` with 3000, and `OrderPlaced` with no `total` at all. How many reach the target?
hint: Every field the pattern names must match, and `>` is strict.

prompt: A partner's system sends bursts of 5,000 orders in a minute, and the database behind the function cannot take that rate. Which trigger fits?

choices.text: A function URL the partner calls for each order
choices.why: Each call runs the function at once, so the burst reaches the database at the partner's rate.

choices.text: An SQS queue read by an event source mapping
choices.why: The queue absorbs the burst and the mapping reads it in batches, at a pace the function and its database decide.

choices.text: An EventBridge rule on the partner's events
choices.why: A rule routes each event as it comes and invokes asynchronously; it does not slow a burst down.

choices.text: An S3 bucket the partner uploads each order to
choices.why: Every upload is its own notification, and the burst arrives as a burst of invocations.

prompt: A function URL is created with `--auth-type NONE`, and every request gets `403 Forbidden`. What is missing?

choices.text: An API Gateway in front of the URL
choices.why: A function URL works without API Gateway; that is its point.

choices.text: Signing every request with SigV4
choices.why: That is what `AWS_IAM` requires; `NONE` means no signature.

choices.text: A statement in the function's policy allowing the principal `*`
choices.why: A public URL also needs the function's resource policy to allow everyone to invoke it through the URL.

choices.text: A destination for failed invocations
choices.why: Destinations belong to asynchronous invocations, and a URL is synchronous.

prompt: The same handler, raising on malformed input, is attached to API Gateway in one account and to S3 in another. A malformed event reaches each. What differs?

choices.text: Nothing: the handler raises the same exception in both
choices.why: The exception is the same; what happens to the event afterwards is decided by the trigger's shape.

choices.text: S3 shows the user an error page; API Gateway retries twice
choices.why: That is the two the wrong way round: API Gateway is synchronous and S3 asynchronous.

choices.text: Both retry twice and then use a destination
choices.why: Retries and destinations are for asynchronous invocations; API Gateway's caller just gets the error.

choices.text: The caller sees the error; S3's event is retried
choices.why: Synchronous returns the failure to the caller; asynchronous queues, retries and gives up to a destination.

prompt: A stream mapping is created with `--starting-position LATEST` an hour after the table began writing changes. What happens to the changes of that hour?

choices.text: The function never sees them; reading starts with the next record written
choices.why: `LATEST` begins after the newest record; `TRIM_HORIZON` would have started with the oldest still kept.

choices.text: They arrive first, then the new ones
choices.why: That is `TRIM_HORIZON`, the setting the section's mapping used.

choices.text: They arrive in one large batch when the mapping starts
choices.why: No starting position gathers the past into a single batch.

choices.text: They are sent to the on-failure destination
choices.why: Unread records are not failures; a destination receives records the function failed on.
